question: How can a piece sound improvised when its metre and phrase lengths are written out exactly?
intro: Night moths open Ravel’s Miroirs: quick chromatic figures that keep stopping and restarting, a slow dark middle section, then a shorter return. All five pieces of this set are one performance, by Olena Havyuk-Sheremet of the Lviv Conservatory.

sections.label: A · Moths in flight — Très léger
B · Pas trop lent — sombre et expressif
Link · The first tempo returns, building
A′ · The opening figure returns
sections.mNote: opening figure restated; metre-shifting passage returns, shorter

cues.title: Night moths, nine bars
cues.text: Noctuelles means night moths. Ravel marks the opening Très léger: quick chromatic figures flutter in the middle of the keyboard while the metre keeps shifting, so the pulse never settles. The first flurry lasts nine bars and ends in a near-silent bar about ten seconds in.
cues.evidence: The first edition (scan p. 1) has nine bars before the first very quiet rest bar, and a published analysis divides the opening into nine-, eleven- and sixteen-bar segments (PTNA Piano Encyclopedia). In the recording the quietest early window is 0:10–0:15 (−31.5 dB against −10.8 dB just before), after which the music restarts.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Fargue and the Apaches
cues.text: Ravel dedicated Noctuelles to the poet Léon-Paul Fargue. Each piece in Miroirs goes to a member of the Apaches, the circle of poets, painters and musicians around Ravel and Ricardo Viñes who met every week from about 1903, often in the painter Paul Sordes’s studio.
cues.evidence: The dedications are listed on IMSLP’s work page and on the first edition; the group’s weekly meetings and the Sordes studio are described in Wikipedia’s article on Les Apaches (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_Apaches).

cues.title: The flutter stops
cues.text: The music darkens and slows. Ravel writes Pas trop lent, sombre et expressif: bars alternate between five and three beats, a detached repeated figure sounds low in the left hand, and long phrases move above it.
cues.evidence: This is the strongest change in the first half of the recording: the report’s boundary at 1:00 scores 0.92, and the onset rate falls from about 3.6 to 0.6 attacks a second. The marking, the 5/4 and 3/4 bars and the repeated left-hand figure are on scan p. 4 of the first edition.

cues.title: Count five, then three
cues.text: Count the slow beat: bars of five alternate with bars of three, so the phrases lean forward before they settle. Through this stretch the recording stays sparse, at one or two attacks a second, and each chord is left to ring.
cues.evidence: The alternating 5/4 and 3/4 bars are on scan p. 4 of the first edition. The report’s onset rate stays between 0.6 and 2.2 attacks a second from 1:00 to 1:35.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Eliminated in the first round
cues.text: In 1905, while Miroirs was being finished, Ravel entered the Prix de Rome for the last time and was eliminated in the first round. Even critics unsympathetic to his music called the result unjustifiable. Gabriel Fauré succeeded Théodore Dubois as director of the Conservatoire that year.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s Maurice Ravel article (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Ravel) describes the 1905 elimination and the critics’ reaction and names Fauré as Dubois’s replacement; the Académie des beaux-arts notice (https://www.academiedesbeauxarts.fr/theodore-dubois) says Dubois directed the Conservatoire until 1905. Whether the affair caused Dubois’s departure is disputed (French Wikipedia on Dubois reports a retirement, not a resignation), so the text states only the sequence.

cues.title: The first tempo returns
cues.text: Around 2:30 Ravel marks the first tempo to return, and the fluttering figures come back in fragments. In this recording the level rises quickly, and the loudest stretch of the whole piece falls between about 2:35 and 2:50, where one figure repeats bar after bar.
cues.evidence: The report shows a boundary at 2:28 (0.56), the onset rate rising from 1.6 to 4.6 attacks a second at 2:35, and the two loudest 5-second windows at 2:35 and 2:45. The instruction “revenez au premier mouvement” and the repeated figure are on scan pp. 5–6; the exact bar is not aligned.

cues.title: The opening comes back
cues.text: From about 3:15 the first figure returns after a near-silent bar, pianissimo, and the metre-shifting passage that followed it at the start comes back in shorter form. Compare its length with the first section’s minute.
cues.evidence: The 5-second window at 3:15 is one of the five quietest in the recording (−23.0 dB), and the onset rate jumps from 2.0 to 4.6 attacks a second by 3:20. Scan p. 7 restates the figure of scan p. 1 and scan p. 8 a passage close to scan p. 3; the return’s start is estimated, not bar-aligned.

cues.title: Ravel on his own harmony
cues.text: In his 1928 autobiographical sketch, dictated to Roland-Manuel, Ravel said that Miroirs marked a change in his harmony large enough to disconcert musicians used to his earlier style. Noctuelles starts the set with chromatic figures that obscure its home key, D♭ major.
cues.evidence: The sketch is quoted in Kyle Fyr, “Mapping Ravel’s ‘La vallée des cloches’”, Music Theory Online 26.4 (2020), paragraph 1 (https://mtosmt.org/issues/mto.20.26.4/mto.20.26.4.fyr.html), citing Orenstein, A Ravel Reader (2003), p. 30. The D♭ major home key is given on IMSLP’s work page.

cues.title: Presque lent, lointain
cues.text: Marked Presque lent and lointain (distant), the fluttering gives way to quiet chords and a slow line marked pp expressif. This is the strongest change in the whole recording: the onset rate falls to about one attack a second and the tone darkens.
cues.evidence: The report’s strongest boundary is 3:52 (1.00). Brightness falls from 1166 Hz at 3:40 to about 560 Hz, and the onset rate to 1.0 a second by 3:55. The markings are on scan p. 9 of the first edition.

cues.title: A last shimmer
cues.text: The first tempo returns one last time: chords repeat pianissimo high on the keyboard in a shimmering rhythm, and a small last fragment fades. In this recording the shimmer is audible around 4:10 and the sound is nearly gone by 4:15.
cues.evidence: The onset rate rises from 0.8 to 4.8 attacks a second at 4:10, then the level drops to −30.4 dB at 4:15; the file ends at 4:19. The “1er Mouvt” and the closing figure are on scan p. 9.

transitions.title: A cascade dies away into slow 5/4
transitions.how: The fluttering section ends with a loud chord held under a fermata, then a very fast descending cascade across both hands that fades to ppp. The next bar is in 5/4, and Ravel marks Pas trop lent, sombre et expressif: the tempo is much slower, the left hand repeats a detached figure low down, and long phrases of chords replace the chromatic flutter. The cascade is the last of the moth music; nothing links the two sections except the silence between them.
transitions.evidence: The recording’s boundary at 1:00 scores 0.92, with the onset rate falling from about 3.6 to 0.6 attacks a second. The fermata chord, the ppp cascade and the 5/4 bar are on scan pp. 3–4 of the first edition (IMSLP #02693).

transitions.title: Low repeated notes, then the flutter returns
transitions.how: The slow section thins out to quiet chords above a low repeated note. Ravel writes “revenez au premier mouvement”, and the first tempo resumes with the fluttering figure now low in the keyboard at ppp, over the same repeated bass note. A crescendo then carries the figure upward to forte, where one pattern repeats bar after bar. The motif is the opening’s, but it returns in fragments under a held bass, not in the opening’s bright middle register.
transitions.evidence: The report has a boundary at 2:28 (0.56) and an onset rate that jumps from 1.6 to 4.6 attacks a second by 2:35. The instruction and the low, quiet restart of the figure are on scan p. 5 of the first edition; the crescendo to forte is on scan p. 6. Exact bars are not aligned.

transitions.title: Rising runs and a silent bar
transitions.how: After the forte stretch the volume falls back to pianissimo, and the writing runs through rising arpeggio figures like those that ended the first page of the score. A bar marked ppp follows, and the opening’s first figure then returns in its original notation, pianissimo. The listener is back at the start without any new transitional material: the join is made of a quiet gap, not a cadence.
transitions.evidence: The level falls from −10.0 dB at 2:50 to −22.9 dB at 2:55; the 3:15 window is one of the five quietest in the recording (−23.0 dB) and the onset rate jumps to 4.6 a second at 3:20. The rising runs are on scan p. 6 and the restated figure on scan p. 7 of the first edition. The start of the return is estimated.

transitions.title: A fortissimo chord, then a distant chorale
transitions.how: The return ends with a fortissimo chord under a fermata. A pianissimo, très léger run of figures follows and dies to ppp. Ravel then writes Presque lent in 3/4. Quiet chords marked lointain (distant) sit above a low sustained bass, and a line marked pp expressif answers them. The flutter is gone: the section is slow and quiet, and the music ends by recalling the first tempo for a few bars.
transitions.evidence: The strongest boundary in the report is 3:52 (1.00); the onset rate falls to about one attack a second and the brightness to about 560 Hz. The fermata chord, the ppp rush and the Presque lent bars are on scan p. 9 of the first edition.

composer.epithet: An engineer of instrumental colour who made a piano imitate water, an orchestra imitate a machine, and old dances carry the names of the dead.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; composition with Fauré from 1897, counterpoint with André Gedalge
Les Apaches: Ricardo Viñes, Maurice Delage, Tristan Klingsor, Michel-Dimitri Calvocoressi and other musicians, writers and painters
Le Belvédère, Montfort-l’Amaury, 1921–37; now a museum preserving his piano and collections
Two operas, two piano concertos, ballets, songs, chamber music and piano works; no symphony

quote.text: Does it never occur to these people that I may be artificial by nature?
quote.source: Ravel, as remembered by his friend M. D. Calvocoressi

composer.background:
Ravel was born in Ciboure, across the harbour from Saint-Jean-de-Luz, to Marie Delouart, a Basque woman who had lived in Madrid, and Pierre-Joseph Ravel, a Swiss-born engineer. The family moved to Paris when Maurice was three months old. His father encouraged music as well as an interest in machinery; his mother’s songs gave him an early acquaintance with Spanish idioms. Basque ancestry and Spanish musical theatre remained distinct resources: the uneven pulse of the Piano Trio differs from the habanera of the Rapsodie espagnole. He returned to the Basque coast for holidays and composition, but received his musical education in Paris.

He entered the Conservatoire in 1889, initially as a pianist, and studied with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot. Failure to win the required prizes cost him his place in 1895. Readmitted in 1897 to Fauré’s composition class, he also learnt counterpoint from André Gedalge. Fauré encouraged the individual ear without relaxing the demands of construction; Gedalge supplied the discipline behind the fugues and independent inner parts. Ravel did not become a virtuoso pianist. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, introduced much of the difficult piano music, including Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit.
